newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's Milosevic invites OSCE to verify elections.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's Milosevic invites OSCE to verify elections.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic offered on Friday to let international observers check the fairness of elections which prompted Western condemnation after opposition parties claimed the vote was rigged.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) welcomed a request from Yugoslavia but warned it could not verify the November local elections.
Instead it could meet all the parties and put up suggestions for getting out of the crisis, OSCE chief spokeswoman Melissa Fleming said.
Hours later, the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition and Belgrade students staged the biggest protest in Belgrade so far.
More than 200,000 students and opposition supporters joined a 26th day of demonstrations, jamming the city centre and adjoining streets.
Belgrade students staged a 20-km (12-mile) march across the city. Students described Milosevic letter to Christopher as "something out of the Twilight Zone".
Zajedno leader Vuk Draskovic rejected the idea of OSCE intervention: "What we want is to be given back what has been stolen from us."
Milosevic, under severe U.S. pressure, protested in a letter to Secretary of State Warren Christopher that Serbia had a healthy democracy and accused Zajedno of "political terrorism".
Milosevic proposed the OSCE should check the November vote in which Zajedno said the socialists suffered their worst defeat in 50 years of unbroken rule.
Zajedno has mounted more than three weeks of peaceful street protests since claiming it was cheated of victory during the local elections by Milosevic's ruling socialists.
Zajedno accused the socialists of stuffing ballot boxes in provincial towns. In Belgrade, the socialists initially admitted defeat before accusing Zajedno of "irregularities" which the courts upheld.
The socialists issued an invitation to the opposition to hold a parliamentary debate on the recent elections and the role of the media.
Zajedno has said it would boycott any dialogue until the results of the ocal elections were reinstated.

Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic, writing to the OSCE, said the invitation had been made "due to dissatisfaction with the election results and the protests staged by a part of the opposition", the OSCE said.

Fleming said nowhere in the letter was the body called on to check the results of the elections, in which the Zajedno opposition said the socialists suffered their worst defeat in 50 years of unbroken rule.
"The OSCE will not be in a position to go to the country and verify the results of the election," she told Reuters.

"What the OSCE could do is send a high-level delegation to meet all interested parties, with the condition that the OSCE has open access to all of them and to make recommendations following that on ways to get out of the crisis," she added.
One Western diplomatic source in Vienna warned the OSCE to tread carefully to avoid being manipulated by Milosevic.
Zajedno was angered by Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini who said in Belgrade on Thursday that it was unrealistic to expect reinstatement of the election result.
His remarks reinforced Zajedno's fear that a backroom deal was being worked out to give Milosevic an escape route.
Political sources said it was probably too late to reinstate the election result without the socialists admitting fraud, which the Serbian leader would not tolerate.
